**Solution 1 (answer 7) is wrong.** It claims every n ≥ 7 works, but n = 7 has a counterexample. Take the 7 complements of the lines of the Fano plane as 4-edges, and add the 7 Fano lines as 3-edges. Any two complements meet in exactly 2 points, so each of the 28 non-line triples lies in exactly one 4-edge. Hence δ₃ ≥ 1.

Now take any 5-set U. Its complement is a pair {a,b}, and the line L through a and b gives a 4-edge Z = [7]∖L ⊂ U, with U∖Z = {c}. In any tight 5-cycle on U, the two windows avoiding c are distinct triples inside Z. Each such triple lies only in the edge Z, so two distinct hyperedges are needed from a single one. So there is no Berge-C₅³. Therefore n₀ ≥ 8.

**Solution 3 (answer 6) is wrong.** Take the 4-edges {1,2,3,4}, {1,2,5,6}, {3,4,5,6} and add the 8 transversal triples of the matching {12, 34, 56} as 3-edges. This gives δ₃ ≥ 1. For any 5-set U = [6]∖{v}, let p be the partner of v. The 4-set Z = [6]∖{v,p} is an edge. Every triple inside Z contains a full matching pair, so it lies only in Z. Any tight 5-cycle on U has two windows avoiding p, both inside Z, and they cannot both use Z. So there is no Berge-C₅³, and n₀ > 6.

**Solution 2 (answer 3) is wrong.** For n = 4, the single hyperedge V has δ₃ ≥ 1 but no Berge-C₄³, so n₀ > 4.

**Remaining issue.** The Steiner quadruple system S(3,4,8) (the affine planes of AG(3,2)) also gives a counterexample at n = 8, so the true n₀ is at least 9. I did not verify whether n = 9 or larger admits a counterexample, so I cannot give the exact value. None of the three proposed answers (3, 6, 7) can be correct, since each is refuted by a counterexample at a size where that answer claims the property holds.

CHOICE: NONE
